source.title: GA-SAM: Gradient-Strength based Adaptive Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Improved Generalization
source.authors: Zhiyuan Zhang; Ruixuan Luo; Qi Su; Xueting Sun

record.tranche_reason: The study trains models with sharpness-aware methods and measures held-out task performance and robustness to parameter corruption, bearing conceptually on the relation between parameter robustness and generalization. It does not test the specific claim versions as written.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for GA-SAM and comparator methods on NLP tasks, and parameter-corruption robustness. Cited results from prior work are not included. Hyperparameter values used only to select configurations are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses a flatness–generalization rationale to develop GA-SAM and evaluates its NLP performance and parameter-corruption robustness. It does not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness ranking of train–test gaps among comparably fitted networks, or any other listed version. Its theoretical argument concerns a broader flatness claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors: their distribution-shift framework motivates GA-SAM, which improves the reported NLP metrics over baseline and tested comparators; robustness and estimated Hessian spectra are interpreted as evidence of flatter minima. Their broad robustness summary needs the Table 4 qualification that GA-SAM has a larger BLEU drop at the smallest L-infinity corruption.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes GA-SAM, which uses gradient-strength-based adaptive corruption scales and a multi-step risk implementation. It evaluates NLP classification, language modeling, and translation, rather than the claim versions' image-classification, architecture, width, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, or memorization settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance depends on task and method: single-step SAM does not improve the LSTM result, and perturbation tolerance changes with the corruption norm and ε. The paper reports that large ε can harm performance.

fits_no_version.finding: GA-SAM improves all four reported NLP metrics over baseline. Ordinary SAM worsens PTB perplexity from 86.70 to 89.66 and slightly improves the other three metrics.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sharpness-aware training can change held-out NLP performance, depending on method and task.

fits_no_version.finding: GA-SAM retains higher corrupted En-Vi BLEU at every tested corruption strength and loses less BLEU in five of six conditions. At L-infinity epsilon 0.0001, its loss is larger: 0.43 versus 0.30.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: GA-SAM usually reduces BLEU degradation under the tested adversarial parameter corruptions.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 5.3 and Figure 3 report lower estimated leading Hessian eigenvalues with GA-SAM, without magnitude normalization or a ranking against generalization gaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: GA-SAM can reduce an unnormalized curvature proxy for sharpness.

fits_no_version.finding: MNIST MLP simulations show similar shifted training and test loss curves near their minima and a correlation of 0.9514 between mixing proportion and parameter-shift magnitude.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the study's simulation procedure, distribution changes can approximately correspond to shifts of local loss minima.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The study does not report train error or train-test gaps, and it does not compare magnitude-aware sharpness measures across similarly trained models. Table 4 reports corruption robustness for En-Vi only; its values do not establish sharpness ranking against generalization gaps.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 also reports ASAM, Layer-SAM, and Multi-step Defense values; omitted to keep the direct baseline, SAM, and proposed GA-SAM comparisons. Table 2 ablation variants and Table 3 hyperparameter sweeps are also omitted because they compare GA-SAM variants or parameter settings rather than testing a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD on the same workloads under specified tuning regimes.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout interventions and interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.

Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance measured through training-error increases; its ranking of train–test gaps among similarly fitted convolutional networks; comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Change V7 from tested_not_extracted to not tested. The analytic trials do show training and test loss curves, so the record's blanket statement that training error is unreported is too broad; they do not supply the matched training-error and generalization-gap comparisons V7 requires. Different base optimizers across different tasks do not constitute a V4 comparison. No omitted result tests a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Network width beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the effect of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning regimes.
Large-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and its interaction with data augmentation and weight decay.

The study measures robustness to L2- and L-infinity-constrained perturbations, but not magnitude-aware sharpness or whether perturbation tolerance ranks train-test gaps among models with similarly low training loss.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
